A five-minute warm-up before Lecture 2.
All of it is from Week 1.

## Bash and the filesystem (Lecture 1)

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Put the commands in order to end up inside a new `projects` folder in your home directory, with `README.md` open in Positron

> You cannot step into a folder that does not exist yet.

1. `cd ~`
2. `mkdir projects`
3. `cd projects`
4. `positron README.md`

## Sort the commands: which only look, and which change your files?

- `mv` :: Changes your files
    > Moves a file or folder: it appears in the new place and disappears from the old.
- `ls` :: Only looks
    > Lists files and folders in the current folder.
- `pwd` :: Only looks
    > Just prints the current path showing where we are.
- `rm -r` :: Changes your files
    > Deletes a folder with all its contents.
- `head` :: Only looks
    > Shows the first lines of a file.
- `cp` :: Changes your files
    > Copies a file or folder, the original stays where it was.

## Where does each command leave you?

Your working directory is `/home/username`.
Some directories are used more than once.

- `cd Documents` :: `/home/username/Documents`
    > Relative: counted from where you are.
- `cd ..` :: `/home`
    > One step up from `/home/username` is `/home`.
- `cd ~` :: `/home/username`
    > `~` is your home folder, from anywhere.
- `cd ./Documents` :: `/home/username/Documents`
    > `./` is the current folder, so this is the same as `cd Documents`.
- `cd` :: `/home/username`
    > `cd` with no argument also goes home.
- `cd /home/username/Documents` :: `/home/username/Documents`
    > Absolute: counted from the root of filesystem, so works the same from anywhere.

## The folder looks empty, but your classmate insists something is in it. What do you run?

1. [x] `ls -a`
    > `-a` lists all entries, including names that start with a dot (hidden files and folders).
2. [ ] `ls -F`
    > Decorates names with `/` and `*`; hidden files stay hidden.
3. [ ] `ls -l`
    > Long listing with sizes, dates and permissions; hidden files stay hidden.
4. [ ] `pwd`
    > Prints where you are, not what is in the current folder.
```

## Git and GitHub (Lecture 2)

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Match each command to the move it makes. (Not all arrows will be used.)

You drew one row per command in lecture: a change moves between
working directory, staging area, repository, and remote.

- After editing `README.md`, you run `git add README.md` :: Working directory → Staging area
    > `add` stages the change: chosen for the next commit, but not on the stack yet.
- `git commit -m "Clarify README"` :: Staging area → Local Repository
    > The sheet goes onto the stack: the staged change becomes a commit with a parent.
- `git push origin main` :: Local Repository → Remote
    > Your new commits go up to GitHub. Nothing on your machine changes.
- `git log --oneline` :: No move: it only reads
    > `log` reads the repository column. Reading commands get no arrow.
- Your teammate pushed; you run `git pull origin main` :: Remote → Local Repository and working directory
    > The mirror of clone: remote commits come down into your repository and your files.
- :: Working directory → Remote
    > No command does this. Edits reach GitHub only through add, commit, and push.
- :: Staging area → Remote
    > Staging is local. Only push talks to the remote, and it sends commits, not staged changes.

> Which column is the change in before the command, and which after?

## Where does each change exist right now?

Some answers apply to more than one situation.

- You saved a file in Positron but ran no git commands :: Working directory
    > Git has not recorded anything yet: the change sits only in your files.
- You edit `README.md` with the web pencil and press the green commit button :: Remote
    > The green button commits inside GitHub's copy. Your clone gets it when you pull.
- You ran `git commit` but have not pushed :: Local repository
    > The sheet is on your local stack. GitHub learns about it when you push.
- A commit you pushed yesterday :: Local repository and Remote
    > Push copied it up; since then both repositories have it.
- `git status` lists a file in red: changed, not staged :: Working directory
    > Red means the change lives only in your files so far; `add` is what stages it.
- Your teammate pushed an hour ago; you have not pulled :: Remote
    > GitHub does not push to you. Until you pull, your clone has no idea.
- :: Classmates' clones
    > Never automatic. Each person's clone changes only when that person pulls.

> Ask which copies of the repository have seen the change.

## SSH setup: which piece goes where?

- The text you paste at github.ubc.ca → Settings → SSH keys :: Public key
    > The padlock: safe to hand out, useless for breaking in.
- The file that must never leave your laptop :: Private key
    > Whoever holds it can push as you. It is never pasted or sent anywhere.
- What actually proves it is you when `git push` runs :: Private key
    > Your machine answers the server's challenge with the private key.
- What you would also add to github.com so a second site recognizes you :: Public key
    > Copy the same padlock to as many doors as you like.
- :: Your CWL password
    > SSH replaces password logins. No step of the setup asks any site for your CWL password.

> One half travels, one half stays home.
```
